cards.back: The process by which the world gets into our minds

cards.front: What is a good way to study perception?
cards.back: By studying how it breaks
Perception is the basis of most thoughts, feelings and actions
Vision sits at the top of the sensory hierarchy - a huge proportion of the brain is involved in vision (far more than the other senses)
That we have to work backwards from sensory stimulation to construct reality

cards.front: What is perception as a constructive act and its two big components?
cards.back: That perception constructs reality by making unconscious inferences about the world, Components =  sensory and top-down.

cards.front: Why do we need top down processing?
cards.back: It helps disambiguate sensory input.
Perceptual boundaries or edges that aren't physically there
The idea that perception cannot be influenced by conscious knowledge
The automatic process of interpreting sensory input.

cards.front: Why should we study visual illusions?
cards.back: Because they reveal things about constructive perception.
That the mind is what the brain does, but the mind doesn’t reduce to the brain.

cards.front: What are David Marr's three levels of analysis?
cards.back: Computational, Algorithmic/representational, Implementational/Physical

cards.front: What is the computational level of analysis?
cards.back: It is the what and why. i.e. logic and environmental constraints. E.g. Arithmetic (for a cash register)

cards.front: What is the algorithmic level of analysis?
cards.back: It is the how. i.e. representations and specific processes. E.g. Arabic numerals and carrying for addition (for a cash register)

cards.front: What is the Implementational level of analysis?
cards.back: It is the where/who. i.e.  How are the algorithms physically materialised. E.g. a notched wheel (for a cash register)

cards.front: What level of explanation is the mind at?
cards.back: The Computational

cards.front: What level of explanation is the brain at?
cards.back: Implementational

cards.front: What are the three main approaches for cognitive neuroscience?
cards.back: Pp (Psychophysics/perception), Ph1 (Stimulus-Physiology), Ph2 (Physiology-perception)
Psychophysics/perception - relationship between physical stimuli and  behavioural response / conscious experience. E.g. reporting differences between stimuli
Stimulus-Physiology -  how neurons are directly reacting to stimuli.
Physiology-Perception - relationship between brain activity and conscious experience.

cards.front: What is EEG, its function and benefits?
cards.back: Electroencephalography - it measures electrical currents in the brain. High temporal resolution, low spatial resolution.

cards.front: What is fMRI, its function and benefits?
cards.back: Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging - measures the flow of blood in the brain. High spatial resolution, low temporal resolution.

cards.front: What is TMS, its function and benefits?
cards.back: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation, creates a temporary lesion by disrupting electrical signals. Allows for causal inferences.

cards.front: Why is the spontaneous firing rate useful?
cards.back: It keeps neural circuits continuously primed, and it allows for inhibition to occur, enabling bidirectional information.
A measure of perceptual sensitivity.

cards.front: What are the two kinds of thresholds?
cards.back: Absolute/detection threshold (minimum stimulus) and relative/discrimination/difference threshold (just noticeable difference).

cards.front: What is the method of adjustment and its benefits?
cards.back: Participants adjust the stimulus until it is barely visible. It allows for quick threshold determination

cards.front: What is the method of limits and its benefits?
cards.back: The experimenter changes the stimulus until detection success changes. It is more reliable than adjustment.

cards.front: What is the method of constant stimuli and what can it produce?
cards.back: It repeats the same stimuli multiple times and tallies detections. produces psychometric curve.

cards.front: What are the four outcomes of a signal detection task?
cards.back: Hit, Miss, False alarm, Correct rejection
Someone's tendency to say yes or no

cards.front: What is method of forced choice?
cards.back: Instead of simply detection, say when or where the stimulus appears, e.g. left or right
The process by which neurons adjust firing patterns in response to continuous stimuli.
It is that the relative threshold is proportional to background stimulus intensity.
The final output cells from the retina; their axons bundle and form the optic nerve
The centre of your retina

cards.front: What is the distribution of rods and cones throughout the retina?
cards.back: Far more cones at the fovea and more rods in the periphery
Where the optic nerve exits the eye

cards.front: What is the computational reason for rods' low-light detection?
cards.back: More rods synapse with a single ganglion than cones, giving a higher sum of input

cards.front: What are parasol and midget cells?
cards.back: Types of ganglion cells; parasol = many synapses, midget = few synapses with photoreceptors
The region of the visual field in which stimulation produces a response in the neuron
Ganglion cells having excitatory centres and inhibitory surrounds (or vice versa)
The inhibition of surround cells in an on-centre cell, which allows for edge detection
The primary visual cortex

cards.front: Where do the visual hemispheres from each eye cross over?
cards.back: The optic chiasm
The Lateral Geniculate Nucleus
That visual fields are processed in different brain hemispheres, not different eyes

cards.front: What is the LGN made up of?
cards.back: Six layers; all are monocular and alternate between eyes. The top four layers are from midget ganglion cells, and the bottom two are from parasol cells
That cells preserve their spatial position

cards.front: How is the retinotopic map in V1 distorted?
cards.back: So that the central 10 degrees takes up almost half of V1
Cells that respond to lines with a specific position and orientation
Cells that respond to lines with a specific orientation but can be anywhere in the cell's receptive field
If the position of a feature shifts, you don't want to lose it
The tendency of simple and complex cells to produce bigger responses with increasing length up to some plateau
End-stopped cells that prefer a line of a particular length
The intensity of an orientation-sensitive cell's firing across different angles

cards.front: What are simple cells made of?
cards.back: Lined-up centre-surround cells

cards.front: What are complex cells made of?
cards.back: Many simple cells

cards.front: What is blindsight, and what does it suggest?
cards.back: The ability for people to report or react to visual stimuli without consciously perceiving it; it suggests visual information has multiple pathways

cards.front: How does feature detection change through V1, V2, and V4?
cards.back: V1 might find edges, V2 might find corners and straight sections, and V4 might observe an entire curve or shape

cards.front: How early are illusory contours occurring?
cards.back: In V2
The 'what' pathway, responsible for identifying what you are looking at
The 'where' pathway, responsible for orientation and spatial information
Damage to the what stream, causing trouble with recognition
Damage to the dorsal stream; a person can recognise objects but has trouble interacting with them

cards.front: What is the third visual pathway sensitive to?
cards.back: Dynamic social cues such as biological motion, eye gaze, and facial expressions

cards.front: What is the static vs dynamic dissociation?
cards.back: Evidence that static and dynamic social cues are processed in different parts of the brain
The brain's ability to perceive an object's colour accurately even when lighting changes; it is based on context

cards.front: What is the timeline of dark adaptation?
cards.back: Over the first 10 minutes, cones fully adapt, then rods keep adapting at a slower rate for up to 30 minutes

cards.front: What else affects lightness perception aside from lateral inhibition?
cards.back: Belongingness and shadow inference - grouping an object onto a specific background or context

cards.front: Why does continuity of a shape matter for lightness perception?
cards.back: Because we make inferences about entire objects
One frequency at one intensity
Light composed of multiple wavelengths

cards.front: How can two different stimuli to a cone produce the same response?
cards.back: Response is determined by photons absorbed; less at a sensitive frequency can equal more at an insensitive frequency
Light (or any sensory input) that are physically different but perceived as the same

cards.front: Why are absorptive and emissive colour combinations different?
cards.back: Because absorbing takes away wavelengths whereas emission adds them
How the retina detects colour - with three cones making up all visible colours
Red-green channels either produce red or green or detect brightness; the same applies to blue and yellow
A cone or two
People with only 1 cone
Where cones work normally but the subject still cannot experience colour

cards.front: What is the difference between perception and perceptual awareness?
cards.back: Perception is the neural process; perceptual awareness is the subjective experience
A subjective experience that differs from the physical stimulus
A stationary stimulus disappears when surrounded by a global moving pattern
Adaptation and prioritizing motion
An ambiguous image with two interpretations, one perceived at a time
Seeing meaningful shapes (e.g. faces) in an unambiguous stimulus

cards.front: What is a Neural Correlate of Consciousness (NCC)?
cards.back: A neural activity pattern that reliably corresponds to a specific percept
Alternating dominance when each eye sees a different image

cards.front: Why is FFA/PPA switching during rivalry a definite NCC?
cards.back: Brain activity switches in step with switches in perceptual dominance (face vs house)

cards.front: What causes dominance to switch in binocular rivalry?
cards.back: Habituation - neurons representing the dominant percept get tired

cards.front: How does exposure length affect rivalry/adaptation?
cards.back: Short exposures prime; longer exposures cause habituation

cards.front: What does unconscious processing during rivalry suggest?
cards.back: Unperceived stimuli still stimulate the brain to some degree

cards.front: What is the traditional approach to explaining perception?
cards.back: Bottom-up processing, increasing in complexity
Sensory input alone is ambiguous / insufficient to specify the world

cards.front: Why does the brain need predictive processing?
cards.back: It only has enough energy to process a few percent of incoming information
Perception is the brain's best statistical guess about the causes of its inputs

cards.front: Is the 'prediction' in predictive processing about the future?
cards.back: No - it's a statistical inference about a current cause, not a forecast

cards.front: What are perceptual predictions based on?
cards.back: Prior knowledge of event likelihood in context

cards.front: What is a prediction error signal?
cards.back: A signal triggered when a prediction is violated, prompting re-interpretation

cards.front: How does prediction error processing save energy?
cards.back: Only violations need processing, not all information

cards.front: What lighting direction do we assume by default?
cards.back: That light comes from above

cards.front: What explains the Lilac Chaser illusion?
cards.back: Colour opponency, apparent motion, Troxler fading

cards.front: What explains the colour cube and 'The Dress' illusions?
cards.back: Simultaneous colour contrast, context integration, colour constancy
Ignoring what doesn't change
Exaggerating changes that matter
Interpretation equals awareness; attention
Limited capacity to perceptually process everything we see
No single definition - a collective name for a host of prioritizing processes
Moving the eyes to bring a region into the fovea
Attending to a region without moving the eyes
Internally-generated, top-down, voluntary attention
Externally-triggered, bottom-up, involuntary/reflexive attention

cards.front: What kind of cue drives endogenous attention?
cards.back: A symbolic, informative cue that can be ignored

cards.front: What kind of cue drives exogenous attention?
cards.back: A physical event onset, uninformative, cannot be ignored

cards.front: How does the build-up/duration of endogenous vs exogenous attention differ?
cards.back: Endogenous: slow build-up, sustained. Exogenous: fast build-up, transient

cards.front: Which type of attention shows Inhibition of Return (IOR)?
cards.back: Exogenous attention
The fovea has more photoreceptors and gets disproportionately more cortical neurons than the periphery

cards.front: Why don't we have fovea-like receptive fields across the whole visual field?
cards.back: The brain would need to be thousands of times larger

cards.front: How many saccades do we make per second/day?
cards.back: 3-4 per second, about 200,000 per day
A relative loss of vision (raised visual threshold) during saccades

cards.front: What does saccadic suppression contribute to?
cards.back: Preventing interference between views and a stable representation of the world
Very small movements during fixation

cards.front: Why are fixational eye movements needed?
cards.back: They prevent retinal adaptation; a fully still image causes loss of vision
Eye movement that maintains a stable stimulus location on the fovea
Noticeable bottom-up stimuli or important top-down features; depends on context

cards.front: What makes something more salient relative to scene schema?
cards.back: Violating prior expectations/schema

cards.front: What is the premotor theory of attention?
cards.back: That covert attention results from weaker activation of the same circuits that control eye movements

cards.front: What evidence supports the premotor theory?
cards.back: fMRI shows similar activation whether attention is overt or covert, and attention deployment precedes eye movements

cards.front: What conditions can eye movements be a signature of?
cards.back: Unilateral neglect and autism
A task measuring detection speed after a valid or invalid spatial/symbolic cue

cards.front: What is the cost/benefit pattern in cueing paradigms?
cards.back: Benefit (faster detection) for valid cues, cost (slower detection) for invalid cues

cards.front: What happens to exogenous cueing at long cue-target intervals?
cards.back: The effect reverses - Inhibition of Return

cards.front: How does endogenous cueing timing compare to exogenous?
cards.back: Endogenous only becomes effective after a delay, roughly when exogenous becomes ineffective

cards.front: What is the spotlight metaphor of attention?
cards.back: Attention highlights a region and can be moved around, like a spotlight

cards.front: What is the zoom lens metaphor of attention?
cards.back: Attention can cover varying sized areas, trading resolution for coverage

cards.front: What can't the spotlight/zoom lens metaphors explain?
cards.back: Why a benefit at the attended location comes with a cost at unattended locations

cards.front: What is the current view of how attention works neurally?
cards.back: Attention changes the baseline activity and tuning of neurons responding to stimuli
Non-spatial deployment of attention that spreads across parts of a cued object
An uncued location is detected faster if it's part of a cued object, versus an equally distant uncued location in a different object
Failure to notice an event we might expect to notice, e.g. the gorilla test

cards.front: What is the capacity model of attention?
cards.back: Attention is a limited resource, similar to fuel
A limit on number/complexity of things we can process/do at once

cards.front: What is the sequential attention hypothesis?
cards.back: That covert attention shifts to a location before overt eye movement follows
Backward saccades during reading that usually go unnoticed

cards.front: How many characters are needed around fixation for normal reading?
cards.back: About 17-20 characters

cards.front: What is task-related knowledge's role in overt attention?
cards.back: It directs where we look, e.g. faces/bodies when identifying people vs background when recalling a scene

sections.name: Memory Intro, STS/LTS, Ebbinghaus & Iconic/Echoic Memory

cards.back: The mechanisms in the mind/brain involved in encoding, storing, and retrieving information
A framework of 4 factors for memory research: participants, materials/events, encoding, retrieval
Learning that occurs without an intention to learn or study

cards.front: What are the two main types of long-term memory?
cards.back: Declarative and nondeclarative memory

cards.front: What is declarative memory made up of?
cards.back: Semantic (knowledge) and episodic (events) memory
Procedural memory, e.g. 'muscle memory'

cards.front: What is the basic proposed memory system flow?
cards.back: External input -> sensory register -> short-term store -> long-term store (with feedback to short-term store)

cards.front: What early distinction did William James propose?
cards.back: Primary memory vs. secondary memory

cards.front: What are the serial position effects?
cards.back: Better recall for items at the start (primacy) and end (recency) of a list
Better recall for items at the start of a list
Better recall for items at the end of a list

cards.front: Why did Ebbinghaus use CVC trigrams?
cards.back: To use meaningless material and minimize prior associations
The reduction in trials/effort needed to relearn material compared to original learning

cards.front: What shape is the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve?
cards.back: It drops quickly then shallows out over time
The time between the study phase and the test phase
Not knowing whether information is available/stored in memory
Information may be available but not accessible/retrievable without the right cue

cards.front: What did Category cues improving recall of items not retrieved in free recall show?
cards.back: That there is an accessibility problem
A temporary sensory store of visual information

cards.front: What did duration judgment studies show about iconic memory?
cards.back: The subjective duration of a flash is longer than its actual physical duration
Reporting all letters in a briefly flashed matrix

cards.front: What did whole report performance show?
cards.back: Participants could only report about one third of letters in a matrix
Reporting only one cued row of a briefly flashed matrix

cards.front: What did partial report reveal about capacity?
cards.back: A higher estimated span of apprehension ~80% than whole report

cards.front: What did delaying the partial report cue reveal?
cards.back: A rapid forgetting curve - performance drops toward whole report levels within about 1 second
A mask presented before the stimulus, causing proactive interference
A mask presented after the stimulus, causing retroactive interference

cards.front: What is the integration explanation of masking?
cards.back: The mask and stimulus become perceptually enmeshed/combined

cards.front: What is the interruption explanation of masking?
cards.back: Processing of the stimulus is stopped and processing of the mask begins

cards.front: How was integration vs interruption studied in a cued task?
cards.back: A circle cue (backward mask) vs a bar cue to indicate which letter to report

cards.front: What did the bar vs circle cue comparison show?
cards.back: Performance was much better with the bar cue than the circle cue (supporting interruption)
A masking effect where a contour near (not overlapping) the stimulus impairs its perception, as with the circle cue
A brief auditory sensory memory store; also called the precategorical acoustic store

cards.front: How to test partial report for echoic memory?
cards.back: Play 3 tracks, a left, right and center track and cue one of them

cards.front: What did whole vs partial report show for echoic memory?
cards.back: Partial report showed a higher estimated capacity than whole report

cards.front: How does the echoic memory forgetting curve compare to iconic memory?
cards.back: Echoic memory decays more slowly / lasts longer than iconic memory

cards.front: What is the stimulus suffix effect?
cards.back: An extra sound (suffix) added after an auditory list interferes with recall of the last items
Recall differs depending on whether items were presented auditorily or visually

cards.front: How does the modality effect typically show up in recall curves?
cards.back: Auditory presentation gives better recall of the last few list items than visual presentation
We want the network to transmit any kind of data; it can be stored and operated on in binary (and is less error prone)
Two nodes and a link
A channel of direct communication

cards.front: What is the most common encoding of text into binary?
cards.back: ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) - 7 bits, 0-127
The lowest layer of a network, in charge of transmission and reception of raw bitstreams over a communication channel; handles synchronisation, error detection and correction
Transforming bits of data into electric/electromagnetic signals to be propagated
Converting electric/electromagnetic signals back into bits of data
The device responsible for modulation, demodulation and synchronisation (a network adaptor / Network Interface Controller (NIC))
Pulse Amplitude Modulation - varying the magnitude of a signal to represent bits
Frequency Shift Keying - changing the frequency of a carrier signal at intervals to represent bits
Phase Shift Keying - changing the phase of a carrier signal to represent bits

cards.front: What are baud rate and bit rate?
cards.back: Baud rate is the speed at which the signal changes (symbols/sec); bit rate is the speed at which bits are transmitted = baud rate x bits per symbol
The maximum rate at which information can be transferred over a channel, measured in bps

cards.front: Why can't we get infinite bandwidth?
cards.back: Signal degradation - the more precisely we try to measure, the more likely errors become

cards.front: What are some sources of signal degradation?
cards.back: Limited bandwidth, delay, distortion, line noise, and their combined effect
Propagation delay - the time it takes a signal to reach the receiver (lag)
It ensures the sender and receiver are aligned so bits can be accurately interpreted
Transmit a separate clock signal, embed the clock within the data itself, or use a preamble signal
It uses start/stop bits
Guaranteeing a voltage transition in the middle of every bit period

cards.front: What are the two types of transmission media?
cards.back: Guided and unguided
When looking at one layer you shouldn't need to worry about how the other layers work; you always get the same signal

cards.front: Ultimately, what does the Physical layer do?
cards.back: Encodes bits onto the transmission medium

cards.front: What are the main properties of transmission?
cards.back: Propagation delay (single bit travel time), throughput (successful transmission rate, Mbps; <= bandwidth), bit error rate (errors per bit)

cards.front: What issues does the datalink layer need to solve?
cards.back: Framing, error detection, reliability, media access control
A sequence of bits that form a unit of data
Using a sentinel character to delimit a frame, and escaping (stuffing) when that character appears in the actual data

cards.front: What are some ways to do framing?
cards.back: Byte/bit-oriented, specifying frame length, or clock-based framing (looking for expected characters at intervals, multiple times)
Redundant data specifying the beginning of a sequence, the end of a sequence, and other info
Sending 3 bits to represent 1 and picking the majority as correct
Sending a parity bit saying whether there is an even or odd number of 1s (or 0s); if it is incorrect, the sequence is corrupted
Transmitting a sum of the data; the receiver also sums the data and compares results
Cyclic Redundancy Check - computes a short value (the CRC) and appends it to the frame for error detection
Forward Error Correction - correcting errors without retransmission
Automatic Repeat reQuest - retransmission on 'no ACK' timeout

cards.front: How can parity be used for error correction?
cards.back: With a matrix, take the parity of rows and columns; if exactly one row and one column have incorrect parity, their intersection locates the error

cards.front: When should you use error correction?
cards.back: When errors are frequent (like wireless) or retransmission is expensive

cards.front: What should you do when a frame is detected as corrupted?
cards.back: Best-effort delivery: discard (when the physical layer is robust). Reliable delivery: request retransmission (when the physical layer is error-prone)
Media Access Control address (EUI-48) - a globally unique identifier assigned to a device's network interface; first 24 bits = manufacturer ID, last 24 bits = device ID

cards.front: What are some ways to do channel partitioning (multiple access)?
cards.back: TDMA (time division), FDMA (frequency division), CDMA (code division), OFDMA (a combination)

cards.front: Why do we want random access?
cards.back: Fully decentralised, no coordination or slot synchronisation needed, simple; with link rate R and M nodes, each can send at rate R/M
Carrier Sense Multiple Access - each node listens to the link and senses whether a carrier is present, i.e. whether the link is idle
Collision Detection - each transmitting node can detect whether another node has also started transmitting, causing a collision
Detect collision, send jam signal, increment collision count, wait a random interval proportional to the collision count
Collision Avoidance - listen to check if the channel is busy, pause and wait, send data, receive ACK

cards.front: Why doesn't collision detection work well with wireless?
cards.back: Some signals can be millions of times more powerful than others, so a quiet signal may not be detected (hidden node problem)
Local Area Network - connected nodes within a limited geographical area
Communication should be fast, inexpensive and reliable over short distances

cards.front: What are the two most popular LAN technologies?
cards.back: Ethernet and WiFi
A Layer 2 component that receives a frame and forwards it to its destination (store and forward); default behaviour is like a hub
A Layer 1 component that repeats symbols on its input to all outputs
Many hosts connected to one switch

cards.front: What does an Ethernet frame contain?
cards.back: Preamble, destination address, source address, type, body, CRC

cards.front: What is Ethernet's level of service?
cards.back: Connectionless (no handshaking), unreliable (no ACKs or NACKs), MAC protocol: CSMA/CD

cards.front: What is in a switch forwarding table?
cards.back: MAC address, port, and time-to-live (to remove stale entries)

cards.front: How does a switch learn its forwarding table?
cards.back: It inspects inbound frames and records the source address and port; if the destination is unknown, it forwards to all ports

cards.front: How can loops occur in Ethernet, and how are they dealt with?
cards.back: A switch floods a frame, another switch receives and floods it again, back to the origin (Ethernet frames have no TTL); fixed with Spanning Tree Protocol
Spanning Tree Protocol - prevents loops by building a spanning tree and sending along its paths (if the path is unknown, send along every path except the source)

cards.front: Matrix shape rules: row, column, and multiplication?
cards.back: Row = 1×n, column = n×1. Multiplying: inner dimensions cancel, outer dimensions give the result shape. (a×b)(b×c) = a×c.
Row (1×n) × column (n×1) = scalar (inner product). Column (n×1) × row (1×n) = n×n matrix (outer product).
Loss = error on a single datapoint. Cost = error over the whole dataset (often includes regularisation penalties).
Adjusting a model's parameters to minimise an objective function (loss/cost) so the model is as accurate as possible.
(1/n)‖y − ŷ‖₂². Squaring makes big errors huge, so it penalises outliers heavily; small errors barely matter.
(1/n)Σ|y − ŷ|. Linear treatment of errors, so it is robust to outliers. Minimised by the conditional median (MSE gives the conditional mean).
A combination of MSE and MAE: quadratic for small errors, linear for large ones.

cards.front: Name the main optimisers and what each adds.
cards.back: SGD (stochastic gradient descent); SGD+momentum (smooths direction); Adagrad (adaptive step, shrinks toward 0 over many steps); RMSprop (moving avg of squared gradients: small steps on large gradients, larger on flat ones); Adam = RMSprop + momentum.
Moves the parameters in the direction of steepest decrease of the loss (the negative gradient), step size set by the learning rate.
Algorithmic: e.g. linear programming, gradient descent. Procedural: heuristic search, genetic algorithms.

cards.front: What is a conservative system, and why does it matter?
cards.back: A vector field that is the gradient of a scalar field. Gradient descent on the scalar (the loss) can then converge to a fixed point.
Scalar field: L: ℝⁿ → ℝ (one number per point, e.g. loss). Vector field: f: ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ. It is conservative if it is the gradient of a scalar field.
A function is convex if the chord between any two points on its graph lies on or above the graph. Any local minimum of a convex function is a global minimum.
Gradient = slope (vector of first derivatives). Hessian = curvature (matrix of second derivatives); H_ij says how the slope in direction i changes as you move in direction j.
f is convex if its Hessian is positive semi-definite (PSD) everywhere.
A matrix A is PSD if vᵀAv ≥ 0 for every direction v. (Follows from g(t)=f(x+tv) having g''(t) = vᵀHv ≥ 0 via the chain rule.)

cards.front: What is ill-conditioning and when does it happen?
cards.back: When d >> n the Hessian is ill-conditioned: many directions have zero gradient (flat) while others are narrow trenches where gradient descent bounces around.

cards.front: How do you fix poor learning from ill-conditioning?
cards.back: Add a regularisation term to the loss (gives curvature/gradient in flat directions), or change the optimiser.
Updating a model as new data arrives, retaining old knowledge while improving. Used when full retraining is infeasible. It is still one learning problem and needs no change to the NN architecture.
Domain-incremental: classes stay the same, input distribution changes. Class-incremental: each new task adds new classes. Task-incremental: task identity is known at training and test time.
The learner loses earlier capabilities when trained on new tasks. (Sometimes forgetting redundant info is good.)
Minimise loss of old tasks (stability) while still learning new ones (plasticity). Can't maximise both.
Naïve sequential (update on current data only); Joint training (all data, even future: upper bound); Frozen model (no updates after the first task); Cumulative (train on everything seen so far).
Preserve past experience. Naïve (none), Bounded (a sample from previous tasks), Full (cumulative: everything).
Elastic Weight Consolidation: penalise updates to parameters that were important for old tasks.
Reserves capacity per task: prune the least important weights, then retrain only the freed weights for the new task.

cards.front: What is RAG and why use it?
cards.back: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: instead of updating network weights, update a document store. Easier to add or change individual facts.
Embed the query as a vector capturing meaning, then retrieve documents whose vectors are most similar.
TF-IDF (bag of words: lexical match) and MiniLM (semantic similarity).
recall@k: is the correct doc in the top k results? MRR (mean reciprocal rank): average of 1/rank of the first correct result; 1 = best, approaches 0 = worst.
Model: maps input to output. Agent: observes to build its input, decides via LLM deliberation, acts via a harness, observes the result, and loops.
Workflow: the developer defines the control flow. Agent: the model defines the flow.
Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI models to interact with tools and data.
Context exhaustion (context window fills up) and false completion (claims the task is done when it isn't).
P(X,Y) = P(X) P(Y|X). Joint = marginal × conditional (either order). It amounts to a factorisation.
P(X) = Σ_y P(X, Y=y) (integral for continuous). Removes a variable by summing over it.
Splitting an expression into parts whose product equals the original, e.g. P(X,Y) = P(X)P(Y|X).
P(θ|D) = P(D|θ) P(θ) / P(D). Posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence. It infers causes from their effects.
The updated probability distribution over the parameters (or latent variables) after seeing the data: P(θ|D) ∝ P(D|θ)P(θ).
Your initial belief about parameters before seeing data, P(θ) (e.g. weights are probably small). It acts as a penalty/regulariser when you do MAP.
P(D|θ): probability of the observed data as a function of the parameters. Not a distribution over θ. For i.i.d. data it is a product over datapoints (a sum after taking logs).

cards.front: What is the evidence / normalisation term?
cards.back: P(D): total probability of the data across all parameter values, from the sum rule. Makes the posterior sum to 1; doesn't depend on θ.
A single point has zero probability; you must use probability densities (and integrate over regions).

cards.front: Why do we like to use Gaussians?
cards.back: (1) Convenient: log-density is a quadratic, so MLE/MAP become least squares, closed-form. (2) Closed under linear maps, products and marginals: posteriors of Gaussian priors × Gaussian likelihoods stay Gaussian. (3) CLT: sums of many independent variables approach a Gaussian, so noise is often well-modelled by it. (4) Fully described by mean and covariance.
N(x; μ, σ²) = (1/(σ√2π)) exp(−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)). μ = mean (centre), σ² = variance (average squared deviation from the mean). It's an exponentiated parabola.

cards.front: What does a linear transformation do to a Gaussian?
cards.back: Stretches, rotates and shifts it, but it stays Gaussian (a linear map of a quadratic is still a quadratic).
N(x; μ, Σ) = (2π)^(−d/2)|Σ|^(−1/2) exp(−½(x−μ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x−μ)). Σ⁻¹ generalises 1/σ². Isotropic: Σ = σ²I (circular contours).

cards.front: Empirical mean and covariance of an n×d data matrix X?
cards.back: Mean m = (1/n)·(sum down the rows), shape 1×d. Covariance Σ_emp = (1/n)(X−m)ᵀ(X−m), shape d×d.

cards.front: Show that the ML mean of a Gaussian is μ_ML = m_emp.
cards.back: log L = −½Σₙ(xₙ−μ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(xₙ−μ) + const. Differentiate w.r.t. μ: ∇ = Σ⁻¹Σₙ(xₙ−μ). Set to 0 ⇒ Σₙxₙ = Nμ ⇒ μ_ML = (1/N)Σₙxₙ = m_emp. (Second derivative is negative-definite, so it's a maximum.)
Σ_ML = Σ_emp = (1/N)Σₙ(xₙ−m)(xₙ−m)ᵀ (harder to derive, but same pattern as the mean).

cards.front: Combining a Gaussian prior and Gaussian likelihood (1-D)?
cards.back: Multiply them: in log space you're just adding parabolas. Result is a Gaussian whose mean is a precision-weighted average, shrunk toward the prior mean, and narrower than either.
The average squared deviation from the mean. Its square root is the standard deviation.
Choose parameters θ that make the observed data most probable: θ_ML = argmax P(D|θ). Equivalent to minimising the negative log-likelihood (NLL).

cards.front: Why use the log in MLE?
cards.back: Turns the product over i.i.d. datapoints into a sum, which is easier to differentiate and numerically stable. Log is monotonic so the argmax is unchanged.

cards.front: MLE recipe (what to do in a question)?
cards.back: 1) Write the likelihood P(D|θ) (product over i.i.d. points). 2) Take the log. 3) Differentiate w.r.t. θ. 4) Set to zero and solve. 5) Check it's a maximum. E.g. Bernoulli with k heads in N flips: log L = k log p + (N−k) log(1−p) ⇒ p_ML = k/N.

cards.front: What is MAP (maximum a posteriori) estimation?
cards.back: θ_MAP = argmax P(θ|D) = argmin [ −log P(D|θ) − log P(θ) ]: the likelihood/empirical loss plus a regularisation penalty from the prior.

cards.front: Difference between maximum likelihood and maximising the posterior?
cards.back: ML maximises P(D|θ) only (data alone). MAP maximises P(θ|D) ∝ P(D|θ)P(θ), so it also includes a prior belief about θ. MAP = ML + penalty; with a flat prior they coincide. MAP is less prone to overfitting.

cards.front: MAP recipe (what to do in a question)?
cards.back: 1) Write the posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. 2) Take −log: NLL + (−log prior). 3) Differentiate, set to zero, solve. E.g. Gaussian likelihood + N(0,σ_w²) prior on a weight ⇒ w_MAP shrunk toward 0 vs w_ML.
Adds a penalty on squared weights: L₀(w) + (λ/2n)Σw². Forces smaller, more distributed weights. It is MAP with a Gaussian prior on the weights.
Adds a penalty proportional to the absolute values of the weights. Penalises non-zero weights equally and drives unimportant weights exactly to zero (sparsity). It is MAP with a Laplace prior.

cards.front: L1 vs L2 weight decay per step?
cards.back: L2 decay scales with the weight's magnitude (shrinks big weights more). L1 subtracts a fixed constant every step. L1 is an embedded feature-selection method.

cards.front: How do you do gradient descent with L1?
cards.back: |w| isn't differentiable at 0, so use the sign function as the (sub)gradient: +1, −1 or 0.
A curve with a sharp pointed peak at zero (and heavy tails). It's the prior corresponding to L1 regularisation.
Penalises absolute differences between adjacent output elements, encouraging smooth/piecewise-constant outputs.
Adding a term to the loss function (or modifying the data) to prevent overfitting.
−log P(θ) is added to the NLL when doing MAP. Gaussian prior ⇒ squared (L2) penalty (weight decay); Laplace prior ⇒ L1 penalty.
Essentially the same thing: the average negative log-likelihood of the data under the model is the cross-entropy between the empirical distribution and the model.
min (or max) f(x) subject to g(x) = 0. f = objective function, g = constraint function (defines a surface S in feature space). E.g. minimise fuel use given a fixed trajectory.

cards.front: How to formulate a problem as a standard equality-constrained problem (template)?
cards.back: 1) Choose variables x. 2) Write what you want to optimise as f(x). 3) Rewrite every 'must equal' condition as g(x) = 0 (move everything to one side). Example: min f = x₁² − 10x₁ − x₂² on the ellipse x₁² + 4x₂² = 16 ⇒ g = x₁² + 4x₂² − 16 = 0.

cards.front: What is a Lagrange multiplier and the Lagrangian?
cards.back: λ is a multiplier per constraint. Lagrangian: L(x,λ) = f(x) − λg(x). Stationary points of L (∇ₓL = 0 and g = 0) are candidate optima of the constrained problem.

∇f = λ∇g. At the optimum the gradient of f is parallel (same or opposite direction) to the gradient of g, i.e. perpendicular to the constraint surface: a point of tangency between a level curve of f and the constraint.

1) Form the Lagrange equations ∂f/∂xᵢ = λ ∂g/∂xᵢ for each i, plus g = 0. 2) Solve for λ (or one variable) in terms of the others. 3) Substitute into g = 0 to find candidate points. 4) Evaluate f at each candidate; the smallest/largest is the global min/max.

cards.front: What does the constraint shape look like for x₁²+x₂²−1=0 vs |x₁|+|x₂|−4=0?
cards.back: First is a circle, second is a diamond. Constraint surfaces are 1-D curves in the 2-D feature space.

cards.front: What are the requirements for Lagrange multipliers?
cards.back: f and g must have continuous partial derivatives (smooth gradients).
min f₀(x) s.t. fᵢ(x) ≤ 0, i = 1..m (inequality constraints) and hⱼ(x) = 0, j = 1..p (equality constraints).

cards.front: How to form an inequality-constrained optimisation problem (template)?
cards.back: Put the objective in f₀ and rewrite each 'at most / at least' condition as fᵢ(x) ≤ 0. Example: minimise x₁² + x₂² subject to x₁ + x₂ ≥ 1 ⇒ f₀ = x₁² + x₂², f₁ = 1 − x₁ − x₂ ≤ 0. Lagrangian L = f₀ + λf₁ with λ ≥ 0.
g(λ,ν) = inf over x of the Lagrangian L(x,λ,ν). It equals −∞ when the Lagrangian is unbounded below for those λ,ν. It is always a lower bound on the optimal primal value.
Primal: the standard minimisation problem. Dual: maximise the dual function over the dual variables (Lagrange multipliers), swapping minimisation for maximisation.

cards.front: What does 'decodable' mean for a code?
cards.back: The code z lets you recover the input x. Just a working assumption: later codes are allowed to discard information (bottleneck).
I(x) = log(1/p(x)). Rare events are more surprising (→ ∞ as p → 0); log makes independent events additive while probabilities multiply.
H(p) = Σ p(x) log(1/p(x)) = E[surprise]: uncertainty of a distribution. Uniform = most uncertain (max, log₂K bits for K options); one certain outcome = 0.
Average code length needed to transmit symbols drawn from p using the optimal code for p. Common events get short codes, rare ones long.

cards.front: Why do very low-p events contribute little to entropy?
cards.back: Each term is p·log(1/p); as p → 0 the p factor shrinks faster than log(1/p) grows, so the contribution → 0.
H(p,q) = Σ p(x) log(1/q(x)): average surprise when data come from p but you believe q. Always ≥ H(p).
KL[p‖q] = cross-entropy − entropy = Σ p log(p/q) ≥ 0 (Gibbs' inequality), zero iff p = q. The extra, unwanted surprise (extra code length) from using q when truth is p.
No. KL[p‖q] ≠ KL[q‖p] in general. The ELBO/VAE uses KL[q‖p] (reverse of the one used for MLE).
p̂: a sum of delta functions, one at each datapoint, each weighted 1/N.
H(p̂, q) = (1/N)Σ log(1/q(xₙ|θ)) = average negative log-likelihood. Minimising it pushes q up at the observed points.

cards.front: Show that max likelihood = minimising KL.
cards.back: KL[p̂‖q_θ] = H(p̂, q_θ) − H(p̂). H(p̂) doesn't depend on θ (data are fixed), so minimising KL over θ = minimising cross-entropy = minimising NLL = maximising log-likelihood.
Log-likelihood = Σ log p(data|θ); maximising it equals minimising log loss = −log-likelihood = total surprisal.

cards.front: One-line summary: entropy vs cross-entropy vs KL?
cards.back: Entropy: how surprised you expect to be. Cross-entropy: how surprised you are using the wrong model. KL: the extra surprise from the wrong model.

cards.front: Three ways to fit a linear model?
cards.back: Optimise (gradient descent), solve in one step (pseudo-inverse), or infer (Bayesian probability theory).

cards.front: Linear regression model, predictor, error and loss?
cards.back: Model: Y = X·W_true + ε. Predictor: Ŷ = XW. Error: ε = Y − XW (same shape as Y). Loss: L = ½tr(εᵀε) = ½ΣΣε²ᵢⱼ (a scalar).

cards.front: Gradient of the linear regression loss?
cards.back: ∇_W L = −Xᵀ(Y − XW) = −Xᵀε. By the chain rule: ∂L/∂w = tr(εᵀ ∂ε/∂w), with ∇_W ε → Xᵀ and ∇_ε L = ε.
Set gradient to 0: Xᵀ(Y − XŴ) = 0 ⇒ XᵀY = XᵀXŴ ⇒ Ŵ = (XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀY. The matrix (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ is the pseudo-inverse.

cards.front: What is the pseudo-inverse and why is it called that?
cards.back: (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ. X is tall (n×d), not square, so it has no true inverse. But (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ·X = I (a left inverse), and it gives the least-squares solution to XW ≈ Y. It plays the role of an inverse, hence 'pseudo'.
Ŵ = (λI + XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀY. Adding λI to the diagonal makes XᵀX + λI always invertible (all diagonal terms > 0) and penalises large weights.
Numerical stability (XᵀX may be singular) and regularisation (shrinks weights, prevents overfitting). It's also exactly the result of a Gaussian prior on W.

cards.front: Why is linear regression an inference problem?
cards.back: We know X and Y and want W: infer P(W|X,Y). This gives a distribution over weights, hence uncertainty (error bars), not just a point estimate.

cards.front: Posterior over W in Bayesian linear regression?
cards.back: P(W|X,Y) ∝ P(Y|X,W) P(W) (X is observed, P(X) is a delta). Graph: X → Y ← W is a collider.
Likelihood: Y = XW + ε, ε ~ N(0, σ_ε²), so p(Y|X,W) = N(Y; XW, σ_ε²I). Prior: W ~ N(0, σ_w²I) i.i.d. on each weight.
−log p(W|X,Y) = (1/σ_ε²)·½tr(εᵀε) + (1/σ_w²)·½WᵀW + const. Gradient: −(1/σ_ε²)Xᵀ(Y−XW) + (1/σ_w²)W = 0 ⇒ XᵀY = (XᵀX + (σ_ε²/σ_w²)I)W ⇒ W_MAP = ((σ_ε²/σ_w²)I + XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀY.

cards.front: Interpret W_MAP: what is λ, and its limits?
cards.back: λ = σ_ε²/σ_w² (noise var / prior var). σ_ε² → 0: back to pseudo-inverse (= ML). σ_ε² → ∞: W → 0 (just the prior).
Σ_map = σ_ε² · ((σ_ε²/σ_w²)I + XᵀX)⁻¹: the '(⋯)⁻¹' part of W_MAP times σ_ε². It encodes remaining uncertainty about the true weights.

cards.front: Predictive mean and variance for a new input x?
cards.back: Mean: y_pred = x·W_MAP. Variance: σ²_pred = σ_ε² + x Σ_map xᵀ (noise + weight uncertainty). Gives error bars, which shrink near the data.

cards.front: How does prediction relate to the sum rule?
cards.back: Predicting Y means marginalising (sum rule) over the unknown W. The linear algebra of the pseudo-inverse does this for us.
W known, X unknown: infer P(X|Y,W) from Y = XW. Transpose: Yᵀ = WᵀXᵀ, reuse Eq. I with Wᵀ playing X: X̂_map = YWᵀ((σ_ε²/σ_x²)I + WWᵀ)⁻¹.

cards.front: Noisy-sensor example of the inverse problem?
cards.back: X ~ N(0,σ_x²), Y = X + ε. MAP x̂ = y/(1+σ_ε²/σ_x²) (shrinks y toward the prior mean 0). Posterior variance σ_x²σ_ε²/(σ_x²+σ_ε²): narrower than both prior and noise (precision-weighted average; cf. Kalman filters).

cards.front: What is probabilistic PCA (pPCA) and an example use?
cards.back: A latent-variable model Y = ZW + ε where low-dim Gaussian codes Z (unknown) generate high-dim data Y through an unknown linear map W. Learns the subspace + noise level. Example: compressing/denoising face images (219 faces → 2-D codes), dimension reduction, generating new faces by walking in code space.

cards.front: How does pPCA use alternating inference (EM)?
cards.back: Initialise W randomly, then repeat: E-step: fix W, infer Z (inverse problem). M-step: fix Z, infer W (Bayesian linear regression). Both use the regularised pseudo-inverse trick, swapping which variable is 'known'.
E: Ẑᵀ = ((σ_ε²/σ_z²)I + WWᵀ)⁻¹WYᵀ. M: Ŵ = ((σ_ε²/σ_w²)I + ZᵀZ)⁻¹ZᵀY.

cards.front: What is the prior used for in pPCA's EM?
cards.back: Priors N(0,σ_z²I) on Z and N(0,σ_w²I) on W appear as the λI terms in the E- and M-steps. They regularise each step (ridge) and anchor the scale of Z and W.
J(Z,W) = ‖Y − ZW‖² + λ_z‖Z‖² + λ_w‖W‖², with λ_z = σ_ε²/σ_z², λ_w = σ_ε²/σ_w². Reconstruction error plus one penalty per prior: a penalised autoencoder.

cards.front: Why does pPCA converge so fast in the faces demo?
cards.back: Both steps are closed-form pseudo-inverses; by iteration 1 W is face-like, and by iteration 2 reconstruction error has essentially stopped changing.

cards.front: Subtlety: pPCA 'as run' in the course vs textbook pPCA?
cards.back: Only posterior means are kept (not full EM using posterior covariance), and W has a prior. So it climbs the joint posterior rather than the evidence. Textbook pPCA has no prior on W (σ_w² → ∞).
An encoder maps input x to a code z; a decoder maps z to a reconstruction x̂. Trained jointly to minimise ‖x − x̂‖². Data x, code z, reconstruction x̂.

cards.front: How does the E-step relate to an autoencoder?
cards.back: Ẑ = Y·W_enc with W_enc = Wᵀ((σ_ε²/σ_z²)I + WWᵀ)⁻¹ (a regularised pseudo-inverse of W, not its transpose). Reconstruction Ŷ = Y·W_enc·W. Encoder + decoder, both linear.

cards.front: Generative model of pPCA vs the autoencoder?
cards.back: pPCA is probabilistic: specifies prior p(z) and likelihood p(y|z), so it gives p(y), a posterior on codes, uncertainty, and can sample new data. The AE is deterministic: encoder + decoder, no probability, nothing to sample from; fitted by minimising reconstruction error.

cards.front: Linear AE trained by gradient descent vs pPCA?
cards.back: Same subspace. AE: network trained by backprop on minibatches, no closed forms (so parts can be made nonlinear), but no p(y). Its loss has no priors so the scale of W is free and it projects exactly, where pPCA shrinks slightly.

cards.front: Why can't you just add a penalty on ‖Z‖² to the AE and retrain?
cards.back: Rescale W_enc → W_enc/c and W → cW: reconstruction unchanged but the penalty ‖Z‖²→0 as c→∞ while W grows. No minimum exists (only an infimum). Fix: also add weight decay on W (the prior on W).

cards.front: Classical PCA vs pPCA: what's the difference?
cards.back: Classical PCA (eigenvectors/SVD) returns an ordered set of orthogonal directions: 1st maximises variance, then remove what it explains and repeat on residuals. pPCA gives only the subspace (orientation arbitrary), plus the noise σ².

cards.front: Why is pPCA/AE blind to rotations?
cards.back: Rotate Z by orthogonal R and W by R⁻¹: ZW is unchanged. So 'first' and 'second' component aren't meaningful. An SVD post-processing step on Ŵ recovers the ordered axes.

cards.front: pPCA/AE give 'the sheet'; classical PCA gives almost the same sheet plus axes. Why 'almost'?
cards.back: The subspace spanned is the same (pPCA's ML solution spans the top principal components), but pPCA's priors/noise model shrink the reconstructions slightly toward the origin (PCA and the unpenalised AE project exactly). So reconstructions differ a little even though the sheet matches, and only classical PCA also fixes ordered axes.

cards.front: Can pPCA or an AE enforce PCA's ordering?
cards.back: Yes, but not automatically: you must explicitly enforce it (e.g. fit direction by direction on residuals, or post-process with SVD).
Walk along a direction in code space (e.g. −2σ to +2σ) and decode. Points are mostly codes never assigned to a training face, so outputs are generated, not reconstructed.

cards.front: pPCA vs NN autoencoder comparison summary?
cards.back: NN finds the same subspace/reconstructions, but has no closed form and can use nonlinear pieces. Loses p(y), probabilities and uncertainty.

cards.front: Generative story of a Gaussian mixture model (GMM)?
cards.back: 1) Roll a (possibly loaded) K-sided die → component k (prior π_k). 2) Draw x from N(m_k, Σ_k). 3) Record both. Gives labelled data (xₙ, cₙ).

cards.front: Fitting a GMM with complete (labelled) data?
cards.back: Partition by class: π̂_k = N_k/N; m̂_k = mean of class-k points; Σ̂_k = covariance of class-k points (empirical estimates, also the ML solution).
r_nk = how much point n belongs to class k. For labelled data it's 1 or 0 and each row sums to 1. Then N_k = Σₙr_nk, m̂_k = (1/N_k)Σₙr_nk xₙ, Σ̂_k = (1/N_k)Σₙr_nk(xₙ−m̂_k)(xₙ−m̂_k)ᵀ.
Generative: models p(x,c) = p(x|c)p(c) and inverts via Bayes: p(c=k|x) = π_k N(x|m_k,Σ_k) / Σ_k' π_k' N(x|m_k',Σ_k').

Generative (c → x): model p(x,c), then invert (Naive Bayes, GMM). Can sample, handle missing data. Discriminative (x → c): model p(c|x) directly (logistic regression, NNs). Doesn't waste effort on p(x) and often classifies better.

cards.front: Derive: 2-class GMM with shared isotropic covariance gives a sigmoid.
cards.back: log[p(c=1|x)/p(c=0|x)] = log N(x|m₁,σ²I) − log N(x|m₀,σ²I) + log(π₁/π₀). Expand ‖x−m‖²: the xᵀx term is identical for both classes and cancels. Left with wᵀx + b, w = (m₁−m₀)/σ². So p(c=1|x) = σ(wᵀx + b).

cards.front: What is LDA (linear discriminant analysis) here?
cards.back: A GMM with shared covariance: the generative model reproduces logistic regression's form, with a hyperplane decision boundary. (Not Latent Dirichlet Allocation.)
The quadratic terms no longer cancel, giving parabolic (quadratic) decision boundaries.

cards.front: K > 2 classes with equal priors and shared isotropic covariance?
cards.back: Pairwise boundaries are hyperplanes; hard classification gives piecewise-linear regions: the Voronoi diagram of the class means.
Repeat until nothing moves: (1) assign each point to its nearest centroid (centroid is 'responsible'); (2) move each centroid to the mean of its assigned points.
Labels cₙ are latent. Beliefs replace facts: r_nk ∈ [0,1] (soft assignments, rows sum to 1). M-step is the same weighted ML update using r as weights.
1) Initialise m_k, Σ_k, π_k. 2) E-step: r_nk = π_k N(xₙ|m_k,Σ_k)/Σ_j π_j N(xₙ|m_j,Σ_j). 3) M-step: N_k = Σₙr_nk, π_k = N_k/N, m_k, Σ_k from r-weighted data. 4) Repeat to convergence.
Responsibility r_nk = p(k|xₙ) during fitting. Posterior ratio p(c=1|x)/p(c=0|x) is the same kind of object, but with all parameters already known (no fitting).

cards.front: k-means as a limit of EM for GMM?
cards.back: Shrink σ² → 0 (shared isotropic): responsibilities become one-hot (hard) so E-step = assign to nearest mean, M-step = recompute means. What's lost is the posterior's width.

cards.front: Can EM get stuck / what if two centres coincide?
cards.back: EM is monotone but only finds local optima (depends on initialisation). Two components drifting together become redundant/degenerate (also, a Gaussian collapsing onto one point gives infinite likelihood).

cards.front: Kernel density estimation (KDE) vs GMM vs k-means?
cards.back: KDE: one Gaussian per datapoint (K=N), shared isotropic σ² (bandwidth), nothing fitted. Table: centres=data & crisp = empirical distribution; centres=data & soft = KDE; fixed K & crisp = k-means; fixed K & soft = GMM.
Like k-means but creates a new centre when a point's squared distance to the nearest centre exceeds λ. λ is the price of a new cluster. Nonparametric (Dirichlet process).

cards.front: Table of models by discrete/continuous c and x?
cards.back: Discrete c, discrete x: Naive Bayes / mixture of categoricals. Discrete c, continuous x: LDA / GMM / discrete VAE. Continuous z, discrete x: VAE with Bernoulli decoder. Continuous z, continuous x: Bayesian linear regression / pPCA / VAE.

cards.front: Parameters θ vs latent variables z?
cards.back: θ: fixed parameters, fitted (written as a subscript, e.g. p_θ). z: one per datapoint, inferred (inside the brackets). Joint: p_θ(x,z) = p_θ(z)p_θ(x|z).
log p_θ(x): the log-likelihood of the data under a latent-variable model. Needs the integral ∫p_θ(x,z)dz, usually intractable.

cards.front: Evidence = ELBO + KL: state and derive.
cards.back: For any q(z): log p_θ(x) = ∫q log[p_θ(x,z)/q(z)]dz + ∫q log[q(z)/p_θ(z|x)]dz = ELBO + KL[q‖p_θ(z|x)]. Derive: multiply log p(x) by ∫q=1, write p(x) = p(x,z)/p(z|x), multiply and divide by q(z) inside the log, split.

cards.front: What is the ELBO and why a lower bound?
cards.back: ELBO = E_q[log p_θ(x,z) − log q(z)]. Since KL ≥ 0, ELBO ≤ log p_θ(x). Tight when q(z) = p_θ(z|x). Computable as an expectation under a q we chose.

cards.front: Why does the EM algorithm work?
cards.back: Evidence = ELBO + KL. E-step: hold θ, set q = p_θ(z|x) ⇒ KL = 0, bound tight (ELBO = evidence). M-step: hold q, raise ELBO w.r.t. θ (this raises the evidence at least as much since KL ≥ 0 afterwards). So the log-likelihood never decreases.

cards.front: What does the EM M-step optimise?
cards.back: The ELBO splits into E_q[log p_θ(x,z)] + H(q); only the first term depends on θ. So the M-step maximises the expected complete-data log-likelihood.
log p_θ(X) rises each iteration: a huge first jump from a bad start, then diminishing but still strictly positive gains (to a local optimum).

cards.front: EM for GMM vs pPCA in ELBO terms?
cards.back: GMM: q(z)=r_nk is the exact posterior, so the ELBO is tight after each E-step. pPCA as run: only the posterior mean is kept (q is a point), so the bound isn't tight and it climbs the joint posterior.
∇_θ log p_θ(x) = E_{p_θ(z|x)}[∇_θ log p_θ(x,z)]. The evidence gradient is the posterior-weighted gradient of the complete-data log-likelihood.
∇log p(x) = ∇p(x)/p(x) = (1/p(x))∫∇p(x,z)dz = (1/p(x))∫p(x,z)∇log p(x,z)dz = ∫p(z|x)∇log p(x,z)dz. (chain rule for log, sum rule, swap ∇ and ∫, product rule.)

cards.front: What does Fisher's identity mean for gradient descent vs EM?
cards.back: A gradient step already contains an exact E-step (the posterior weighting arises from differentiation). So EM and gradient ascent climb the same hill; gradient descent doesn't skip the E-step, it does it implicitly.

cards.front: Two learning styles: alternate vs just descend?
cards.back: Alternate: infer codes, refit model, repeat (EM). Just descend: one objective, gradients on everything at once (autoencoders). With Fisher's identity both climb the same likelihood.

cards.front: Why is a deep-decoder latent model hard to train directly?
cards.back: log p_θ(x) = log∫p_θ(x|z)p(z)dz is intractable for a neural-net decoder, and the posterior p_θ(z|x) has no closed form.

Restrict q to a tractable family Q and find the best approximation by maximising the ELBO: argmin KL[q‖p(z|x)] ⇔ argmax ELBO. Compared to EM (exact E-step) and MCMC (exact samples, slow), VI is approximate but fast.
A single encoder network q_φ(z|x) with shared parameters φ gives an approximate posterior for every x, instead of solving a fresh inference problem for each x. A separate choice from VI itself.
ELBO = E_{q_φ(z|x)}[log p_θ(x|z)] − KL[q_φ(z|x)‖p(z)]. Reconstruction term (an autoencoder loss) minus a KL regulariser toward the prior N(0,I).
E_q[log p(x|z) + log p(z) − log q(z|x)] (log of a product/quotient) = E_q[log p(x|z)] − E_q[log q/p(z)] (linearity) = reconstruction − KL (that ratio inside E_q is the KL by definition).

cards.front: Role of the KL term / what if you drop it?
cards.back: Pushes encodings toward the prior, keeping the latent space smooth and well-organised (closed form for diagonal Gaussians). Dropping it gives a plain autoencoder: codes scatter, with holes, so sampling from the prior won't decode to plausible data.

Encoder outputs μ_z and Σ_z (diagonal); sample z ~ N(μ_z, Σ_z); decoder maps z → x̂. Loss = −ELBO. Σ is diagonal because positivity is easy (e.g. exp of a log-variance output) vs enforcing positive-definiteness.
Problem: can't backprop through a random sampling step. Fix: z = μ_φ(x) + Σ_φ(x) ⊙ ε, ε ~ N(0,I). z is now a deterministic function of φ (given ε), so ∇_φ flows.
Linear encoder q(z|x) = N(xW_enc, Σ_enc diag) and linear decoder p(x|z) = N(zW_dec, σ²I): the decoder is exactly pPCA's generative model.

cards.front: Four ways to train linear codes: PCA, linear AE, pPCA, linear VAE?
cards.back: PCA: point code, closed form (eigenvectors), subspace + axes. Linear AE: point, gradient descent, subspace only. pPCA: Gaussian, EM, subspace + σ². Linear VAE: Gaussian, SGD on ELBO, subspace + σ² + axes (diagonal q fixes axes).

cards.front: Why were VAEs a big deal?
cards.back: Reparameterisation allows end-to-end SGD through sampling; bridges probabilistic models and deep learning; principled generative view of AEs; smooth structured latent space (interpolate/sample). ELBO-as-objective underpins later generative models (flows, VQ-VAE, latent diffusion).
The likelihood p(x|z) maps code → data (decoder). Bayes' rule inverts it to the posterior p(z|x), whose mean/mode, computed as a function of x, is an encoder (got by Bayes, not trained).

cards.front: Continuous Gaussian prior gives what encoder?
cards.back: Posterior mean E[z|x] = ((σ²/σ_z²)I + WWᵀ)⁻¹ W x: a linear layer, i.e. a regularised pseudo-inverse of W.

cards.front: One-of-K prior: what is the model?
cards.back: z is one of the K one-hot vectors, each with prior 1/K. Rows of W ∈ ℝ^{K×d} are the means m_k. Decoding is a table lookup (embedding table); x ~ N(m_k, σ²I). Marginal is a GMM with equal weights and shared isotropic σ².

cards.front: Derive: the posterior of a one-of-K code is a softmax.
cards.back: p(k|x) ∝ N(x;m_k,σ²I) (flat prior). Expand ‖x−m_k‖² = ‖x‖² − 2m_kᵀx + ‖m_k‖². The ‖x‖² term is the same for all k, so cancels. Left: r_k(x) = softmax_k(a(x)/σ²), a_k = m_kᵀx − ½‖m_k‖².
Components are isotropic and share one σ². (Equivalent to softmax shift-invariance: adding a constant to all logits changes nothing.)

cards.front: Softmax encoder as a neural layer?
cards.back: Linear map with weight rows m_k, bias b_k = −½‖m_k‖², softmax over K units, logits divided by σ² (temperature). Bigger noise ⇒ higher temperature ⇒ flatter code.
x̂ = Σ_k r_k(x) m_k = Wᵀr(x): a posterior mean, with tied weights (encoder uses W, decoder Wᵀ). Code = vector of responsibilities.

cards.front: Why must the reconstruction lie in the convex hull of the m_k?
cards.back: r_k ≥ 0 and Σr_k = 1, so x̂ is a convex combination of the rows. An input far outside the hull is pulled back inside (onto/near a row or boundary): it can't be reconstructed faithfully.

cards.front: Continuous vs one-of-K code, side by side?
cards.back: Prior: Gaussian vs uniform on one-hots. Posterior: Gaussian vs categorical. Code: posterior mean vs whole posterior. Encoder weights: pseudoinverse of W vs W itself + bias. Reconstruction: projection onto a subspace vs point in hull of rows. Marginal p(x): one Gaussian vs mixture of K Gaussians.

cards.front: What does σ² do in the softmax AE?
cards.back: Small σ²: responsibilities near one-hot, x̂ ≈ nearest row (hard code, k-means-like). Large σ²: soft codes, modes of p(x) leave the rows and neighbouring ones merge into blends; at very large σ² a single mode remains.

cards.front: Three ways to fit W in the softmax AE?
cards.back: 1) EM (GMM, closed-form batch, monotone). 2) Gradient ascent on log p(x) (marginal in closed form; update m_k ← m_k + η r_k(x)(x − m_k)). 3) Gradient descent on reconstruction ‖x − x̂‖². The first two optimise the same objective; the third a different one.

cards.front: Reconstruction error vs likelihood: why different optima?
cards.back: Reconstruction error has no noise term, so it fits a noiseless model to noisy data. Since x̂ lies in the hull, minimising squared error drags the rows outward (more so as σ grows) to compensate, whereas max likelihood has σ² absorb the scatter.

Generative: prior p(z) + likelihood p(x|z); gives p(x) and a posterior; can sample; fit by max log p(x). Autoencoder: encoder x→z + decoder z→x̂; gives reconstruction; nothing to sample from; fit by min ‖x−x̂‖².
Store patterns {m_k}; given a noisy/partial query x, return the stored pattern it most resembles. Address by content, like a fragment of a tune retrieving the whole tune.

Binary polar patterns xᵢ ∈ {−1,+1}ᵈ, single weight matrix J with Hebb's rule ΔJ_ij = xᵢxⱼ. Retrieval: update neurons as perceptrons (sign of weighted input). Each update never increases an energy E(ξ); stored patterns are local minima (attractors).
About 0.14·d patterns for d neurons (linear in d, small constant). Also has false 'fictitious' memories (spurious minima).

T(x) = x̂ = Wᵀr(x). Repeated application x → T(x) → … converges to modes of p(x), which sit at (or near) stored rows. A corrupted row walks to its clean original with no denoising training. Retrieval = mode-finding.
x̂ = x + σ²∇ₓ log p(x). Because ∇ₓ log p(x) = Σ r_k (m_k − x)/σ² = (x̂ − x)/σ². Each application of the map is a gradient-ascent step of size σ² on log p.

cards.front: Why does the iteration converge and stop?
cards.back: It is gradient ascent on log p, and stops exactly where x̂ = x (gradient zero), i.e. at a mode.

cards.front: Energy function of the modern Hopfield network?
cards.back: E(x) = −log p(x) = ‖x‖²/(2σ²) − LSE(a(x)/σ²). Then x̂ = x − σ²∇E(x): descending energy = climbing density. LSE's gradient is a softmax, so the pull is competitive, giving much higher capacity than the quadratic 1982 energy.

Small σ²: every stored item is its own fixed point (lookup table; only returns what it was given). Larger σ²: nearby items merge into blends never stored: spurious memories (bad) or generalisation/composition (good).

219 stored faces. Small σ²: 218 fixed points. By σ²≈6: 2 broad prototypes absorb almost all faces. From pure noise at large σ²: converge to the same blend (~average face); at small σ² to a stored face.

Start large and shrink σ² each step: blend sharpens and commits to one face, but the start is forgotten, so deterministic (same face every time). Adding fresh noise each step gives different faces per run; still only samples the training set (no new faces).

No single energy is being climbed. Output stays in the convex hull so it's bounded, but behaviour is open. E.g. decoder rows shifted by one gives cycles m₁→m₂→…→m_K→m₁: a sequence memory (pattern-completion becomes sequence-completion).
∇ₓ log p(x): a vector field (same shape as x) pointing uphill on log p. Not a number or 'scoring'. Distinct from Fisher score ∇_θ log p.

cards.front: Why doesn't the score need the normalising constant?
cards.back: p = p̃/Z ⇒ log p = log p̃ − log Z, and log Z is constant in x, so ∇ₓ log p = ∇ₓ log p̃. Matters for associative memory: recall only needs the unnormalised density.
∇ₓ log N(x; m, σ²I) = (m − x)/σ²: the 'arrow home'. A step of σ² times it lands exactly on m (only true for a single Gaussian).

cards.front: Derive Tweedie for a mixture (3 steps).
cards.back: 1) Shift invariance of softmax ⇒ r_k = softmax(a/σ²). 2) Fisher's identity: ∇log p(x) = Σ_k p(k|x)∇log p(x,k) = Σ r_k(m_k − x)/σ². 3) Multiply by σ²: σ²∇log p = Σr_km_k − x = x̂ − x ⇒ x̂ = x + σ²∇log p_σ(x).

cards.front: Why can't we just use Tweedie directly for large datasets?
cards.back: r_k(x) compares x with every training item: you must hold the whole dataset in memory and use all of it each step.

cards.front: Why does MSE training give the posterior mean?
cards.back: Target is m_k with probability r_k(x). Loss Σr_k‖m_k − D(x)‖²; gradient −2Σr_k(m_k − D) = 0 ⇒ D(x) = Σr_k m_k = x̂ (since Σr_k=1). Absolute error would give the median instead.

Train a net D_θ to predict the clean x₀ from x = x₀ + σε with MSE. Optimum = posterior mean x̂, so score ≈ (D_θ(x) − x)/σ². Ordinary regression on (noisy, clean) pairs recovers the score without evaluating any density. Basis of diffusion.

cards.front: Posterior mean vs displacement vs score?
cards.back: Posterior mean x̂ = Σr_km_k (a point; what the net outputs). Displacement Δx = x̂ − x (the arrow). Score = Δx/σ² (differs by a factor σ²). 'Network computes the score' is shorthand.

cards.front: Three ways to wire the denoiser?
cards.back: Predict the clean point x̂; predict the residual Δx (output = σ²·score, with skip connection); predict the noise ε̂ (score = −ε̂/σ). Same function essentially; diffusion implementations usually predict the noise.

cards.front: Why can't the exact minimiser generate new data?
cards.back: On a finite training set the exact denoiser's x̂ returns the nearest training item as σ → 0, so reverse diffusion just reproduces the training set. Trained networks generalise because they fall short of the exact minimiser (their inductive bias smooths between items). Open question; no general account.

One network D_θ(x̃, σ) denoises at every noise level, with σ as an explicit input (sinusoidal embeddings) since the score field changes shape with σ. Normalise inputs by 1/√(1+σ²) (exact). Loop it with σ annealed from large to small.

cards.front: Why re-add noise at each step of the sampler?
cards.back: Each denoiser expects inputs of 'clean + σ-noise'; the reconstruction x̂₀ isn't like that. Re-noising puts the next input back in distribution. Using the network's own noise estimate instead of fresh noise gives deterministic DDIM.

cards.front: Faces: exact vs learned denoiser result?
cards.back: Learned MLP (5.5M params, 40k Adam steps) ends on a stored face 72/100 runs (55 distinct faces); mostly returns training faces. New faces would likely need far more data.

Representations exist because they help a system predict its sensory input. Top-down prediction vs bottom-up input; the prediction error drives perception, run as error-correction loops. 'Predict' = reconstruct current input OR forecast future input.

cards.front: Two ways to judge a representation?
cards.back: Does it predict (reconstruct/forecast/solve task well; can be dense and inscrutable)? Does it have interpretable structure (sparse, meaningful units: the Barlow/efficient-coding tradition)? Not fundamentally separate: a code capturing real independent causes generalises better.

Sensory systems reduce redundancy to represent the world efficiently. Modern interpretability (sparse autoencoders, probes, steering) partly tries to recover this structure from predictively trained networks.
Distributed: many units participate, information lives in the pattern of weights (Willshaw's associative memory). One-hot-ish: individual units mean something (cf. 'grandmother cell').
Minimising KL to the empirical distribution; the loss was always a cross-entropy.
Penalties. A Gaussian prior on weights is a squared penalty; weight decay is a prior.
A likelihood is a decoder; its posterior is an encoder, got by Bayes' rule, not trained.
A shared-covariance mixture has a softmax posterior, linear in x: the generative model reproduces the discriminative one.
Narrow the Gaussians (σ² → 0) and responsibilities go one-hot. k-means is the zero-noise limit; what's lost is the posterior's width.
Penalised autoencoder: reconstruction error + one penalty per prior (λ_z, λ_w from the prior variances).

7: log p = ELBO + KL, bound tight iff q = posterior. 8: EM climbs it (E closes the gap, M raises the bound). 9: Fisher's identity: a gradient step contains an exact E-step, so EM and gradient ascent climb the same hill.

10: when the posterior is out of reach, pick a family for q and optimise the bound. 11: amortising q into one network is a second, separate choice. 12: gradients can't pass through a sample ⇒ reparameterisation.

13: the objective determines what's pinned down (pPCA: subspace + σ²; linear VAE adds axes). 14: each softmax-AE piece follows from an assumption (one-of-K ⇒ softmax; Gaussian noise ⇒ bias and 1/σ²; Bayes ⇒ tied weights). 15: reconstruction = posterior mean (stays in convex hull). 16: reconstruction error ≠ likelihood (fits a noiseless model; pushes rows outward).

17: iterating the map = gradient ascent on log p; energy = −log p. 18: σ² decides lookup vs blends. 19: squared error learns the conditional mean. 20: with Gaussian noise that mean gives the score, so regression on noisy/clean pairs recovers it. 21: the exact minimiser memorises; the shortfall of trained nets lets them generalise.

cards.front: Theme: starting with the decoder; three ways to get the encoder?
cards.back: 1) Bayes provides it in closed form, nothing trained (pPCA, GMM, softmax AE; tool: EM). 2) Bayes unavailable, so train an approximate second network q (VAE; tool: ELBO). 3) Do without a code at all: one network learns the score (denoising; tool: score matching).

cards.front: Two kinds of code in the course?
cards.back: Continuous Gaussian code (pPCA, linear AE, VAE): density describes a 'trend' (linear or curved). One-of-M code (GMM, softmax AE, associative memory): density describes 'blobs'. A trained denoiser commits to neither.

cards.front: Practice: What happens to GMM responsibilities as σ² → 0 (shared isotropic)? E and M steps?
cards.back: Responsibilities become hard one-hot (nearest mean wins). E-step = assign each point to its nearest mean; M-step = set each mean to the average of its assigned points. That is k-means.

cards.front: Practice: write λ for MAP linear regression with noise σ² and prior w ~ N(0, σ_w²I).
cards.back: λ = σ²/σ_w² (minimise ‖y − Xw‖² + λ‖w‖²).

cards.front: Practice: squared error with two targets (input itself vs clean item): what does each optimum compute?
cards.back: Target = input (fitting softmax AE to noisy data): drags rows outward; fits a noiseless model; does not recover the clean items. Target = clean item (denoiser): optimum = posterior mean E[clean|noisy] = x̂ (via Tweedie, the score), which recovers the clean items. Only the second does.
